strengths: Proposes a conceptually clean alternative to iterative densification in 3DGS: triangulating dense 2D correspondences (from a pretrained matching network) across neighboring views to directly initialize a dense set of well-placed, well-colored Gaussians, removing the need for the incremental split/clone densification loop.

The initialization is compatible with and orthogonal to other 3DGS acceleration/quality techniques (demonstrated by combining with Taming-3DGS), making it a plug-in enhancement rather than a competing pipeline.

Extensive quantitative evaluation across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) against a wide range of quality-focused (3DGS-MCMC, Mip-Splatting, Scaffold-GS, AbsGS) and speed-focused (EAGLES, 3DGS-LM, Taming-3DGS, gsplat, Mini-Splatting) baselines, with consistent gains in SSIM/LPIPS, fewer Gaussians (~40-60% fewer), and comparable or better PSNR.

Good set of diagnostic ablations: Gaussian travel-distance/convergence-path analysis (Fig. 5) that gives mechanistic insight into why dense initialization speeds convergence, robustness-to-noise study on coordinates vs. color, comparison across different dense-matching networks (RoMa/LoFTR/DKM/RAFT) and against a depth-based initialization, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (number of reference views/keypoints).

Reasonable qualitative evidence (Fig. 3, extreme-viewpoint rendering in Fig. 4, extensive supplementary figures) supporting claims of reduced blur and fewer stretched/floater Gaussians away from training viewpoints.
Reports per-scene results in supplementary material, aiding reproducibility and scrutiny of variance across scenes.
weaknesses: The initialization overhead depends on running a heavy pretrained dense-matching network (RoMa) over many reference/neighbor image pairs; although this cost is folded into reported training time, the paper gives limited analysis of how this cost scales with dataset size (number of images, resolution) beyond the mip-NeRF360 setting, which raises questions about scalability to larger or more image-dense capture sessions.

PSNR gains are comparatively modest relative to SSIM/LPIPS gains (as acknowledged by the authors, attributed to view-dependent color/reflectance issues), but this limitation is not quantitatively analyzed per-scene or mitigated, leaving open whether the method underperforms specifically in reflective/specular scenes.

Some baseline comparisons in Table 1 are noted as taken directly from original papers due to unavailable/non-functioning code, and the authors note that re-evaluated mean values for Scaffold-GS and 3DGS-MCMC changed substantially from originally reported numbers; this introduces some uncertainty about the fairness/consistency of head-to-head comparisons.

The core technical contribution (dense correspondence + linear least-squares triangulation for initialization) is methodologically straightforward and shares conceptual similarity with existing depth/NeRF-based initialization strategies (e.g., RadSplat, DepthFM ablation); the novelty lies mainly in the combination and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The neighbor-selection and aggregation heuristics (e.g., choosing top-1 nearest neighbor per reference view, thresholds for keypoint counts/reference views) appear to be manually tuned based on empirical sweeps (Fig. 7) without clear guidance on how these would generalize to substantially different capture setups (e.g., sparse-view, very large-scale scenes) beyond the brief front-facing demo mentioned in the supplementary.

Evaluation is restricted to the same three standard, relatively small-scale benchmark datasets used by prior 3DGS papers; no evaluation on larger/outdoor unbounded scenes, dynamic scenes, or truly sparse-view settings is provided to test the boundaries of the claimed 'dense correspondence' benefit.

The paper would benefit from an explicit breakdown of initialization time vs. optimization time per scene (only aggregate training times are given), which is important for practitioners deciding whether the upfront correspondence computation is worthwhile for their use case.

strengths: The core idea—replacing 3DGS's iterative gradient-driven densification with a one-shot dense initialization obtained by triangulating dense 2D correspondences from a pretrained matcher (RoMa)—is a clean, well-motivated alternative to the standard SfM-sparse-point initialization, and is clearly explained with the projective triangulation formulation (Eqs. 3-8).

The evaluation spans three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) and compares against a wide and relevant set of baselines across quality-focused, speed-focused, and NeRF-based categories, with consistent reporting of training time and Gaussian counts alongside PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough for this class of paper: sensitivity to the choice of dense matcher (RoMa vs LoFTR vs DKM vs RAFT), robustness to synthetic coordinate/color noise, the necessity/redundancy of densification after this initialization, hyperparameter sensitivity (number of reference views/keypoints), and analysis of Gaussian travel distance during optimization (Fig. 5) that directly supports the mechanistic claim of a shorter optimization path.
The method is shown to be modular/orthogonal to other acceleration techniques (demonstrated by combining it with Taming-3DGS), which increases its practical value beyond a single fixed pipeline.

Reasonable transparency about limitations: the paper explicitly reports that densification remains useful in under-reconstructed regions (e.g., the treehill scene) and that the method is comparatively weaker for view-dependent/reflective content, rather than hiding these cases.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: two-view linear triangulation (DLT-style least squares) is classical, and the overall recipe amounts to substituting off-the-shelf dense correspondence (RoMa) for SfM sparse points to seed 3DGS, plus simple heuristics for color/scale initialization. The conceptual leap beyond 'denser initialization helps' is limited.

The paper's framing ('eliminate densification', 'a fundamentally different approach') is partly undercut by its own ablation (Sec. 4.5, Table 2, Fig. A5), which shows densification is still needed/helpful in sparsely covered regions (e.g., treehill) — the title/claims oversell what is actually a substantially-reduced-need-for, not fully eliminated, densification process.

The pipeline introduces a nontrivial dependency on a pretrained dense matching network and requires computing dense correspondences across many reference/neighbor image pairs; although preprocessing time is included in reported numbers, there is limited analysis of how this cost scales with the number of input images/scene size, which is important for the method's practicality on larger scenes/video-like captures beyond the tested benchmarks.

Some reported statistics are hard to reconcile across sections: the paper claims ~40% fewer Gaussians overall, yet per-scene appendix tables (e.g., Table A4) show the Taming-3DGS+Ours variant using more splats than typically reported for standard 3DGS on scenes like bicycle/garden, making the aggregate 'fewer Gaussians' claim less transparent without scene-by-scene context in the main text.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided for the quantitative results, and qualitative comparisons in the main paper rely on cropped regions of interest (full images relegated to supplementary), which limits independent verification of the extent of improvement.

The method's initialization quality is fundamentally bounded by the dense matcher's coverage and accuracy in low-texture, repetitive, or reflective regions; while some robustness analysis is given (synthetic noise), no failure-case analysis is shown for realistic matcher failures (e.g., textureless walls, sky) which are common in the outdoor scenes used.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated question—whether densification can be eliminated entirely by seeding 3DGS with a dense, well-distributed set of Gaussians derived from triangulated dense 2D correspondences—rather than incrementally growing Gaussians via gradient-based splitting.

The triangulation-based initialization is formulated clearly and rigorously (least-squares solution for 3D position from multi-view correspondences, color/scale initialization scheme), and the paper provides sufficient mathematical detail (Eqs. 1-8) for reproducibility of the core algorithm.

Strong and fairly broad empirical evaluation across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), comparing against both quality-focused (Mip-Splatting, 3DGS-MCMC, ScaffoldGS, AbsGS) and speed-focused (EAGLES, 3DGS-LM, Taming-3DGS, MiniSplatting) baselines, with training time and Gaussian count reported alongside standard image-quality metrics.

Thoughtful ablation studies: robustness to synthetic coordinate/color noise, sensitivity to matching algorithm choice (RoMa vs. LoFTR/DKM/RAFT vs. monocular depth-based initialization), hyperparameter sensitivity (number of reference views/keypoints), and a clear analysis of reduced Gaussian travel distance during optimization (Fig. 5) that supports the claimed mechanism (shorter optimization path).

Demonstrated compatibility/orthogonality with other 3DGS acceleration techniques (e.g., combined with Taming-3DGS), which increases practical value as a plug-in improvement rather than a competing pipeline.

Extensive supplementary material with per-scene breakdowns, qualitative visualizations, and additional analyses (keypoint aggregation, undercovered regions, noise visualization) that support transparency of the reported gains.
weaknesses: The pipeline's reliance on known camera poses is not fully clarified: it is unclear whether camera extrinsics/intrinsics are still obtained via a full SfM pipeline (e.g., COLMAP) even though the sparse point cloud is discarded, which affects the fairness of speed comparisons and overall reproducibility/practicality claims.

The cost of running a dense matching network (RoMa) over many neighboring image pairs (180 reference views × top-K neighbors × up to 15,000 keypoints per frame) is included in reported times, but the breakdown between matching cost, triangulation cost, and optimization cost is not clearly separated, making it hard to assess how the approach would scale to much larger scenes or sparser-view settings.

Quantitative gains in PSNR are relatively modest compared to gains in SSIM/LPIPS (Table 1), and for the 30k-step 'quality' comparison the improvements over strong baselines like Mip-Splatting/3DGS-MCMC are sometimes marginal or mixed, which somewhat tempers the 'outperforms all' framing in the text.

Hyperparameters (number of reference views, keypoints per view, top-1 neighbor selection) appear tuned specifically to the Mip-NeRF360-scale captures used in the main experiments; the paper only briefly mentions sparse/front-facing applicability in the supplementary without quantitative results, leaving generalization to substantially different capture regimes (very sparse views, extremely large-scale scenes) unverified.

The core idea of leveraging dense correspondence/matching networks for improved Gaussian initialization has conceptual overlap with prior pose-free/sparse-view Gaussian splatting works cited in related work (e.g., InstantSplat, MVSplat, DepthSplat); the paper could more explicitly delineate what is technically novel about its triangulation-based formulation versus these related efforts beyond the specific application to eliminating densification in the dense multi-view setting.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: replacing the slow, incremental densification process in 3DGS with a one-shot, dense geometric initialization derived from multi-view correspondences.

The method is technically well-formulated: a clear triangulation procedure from dense correspondences (closed-form linear system for 3D position), a principled confidence/reprojection-based sampling scheme to select reliable, spatially uniform points, and a spherical-harmonics initialization scheme using multi-view color observations solved via least squares/pseudoinverse when observations are limited.

Extensive empirical validation across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), with comparisons to a wide range of recent efficiency- and quality-focused 3DGS variants (3DGS-MCMC, ScaffoldGS, AbsGS, Mip-Splatting, Taming 3DGS, EAGLES, 3DGS-LM, gsplat).

Demonstrated plug-and-play compatibility: showing that EDGS initialization can be combined with existing ADC/densification methods (3DGS-MCMC, AbsGS, ScaffoldGS, Mini-Splatting) to further improve quality without added Gaussian count or training time, which strengthens the claim of general usefulness beyond just being a standalone pipeline.

Thorough ablations and analyses: matching-algorithm choice, sampling-distribution components, SH initialization, sensitivity to number of reference/neighbor views and correspondences, and quantitative/qualitative robustness to synthetic initialization noise, all of which support the core claims about why the method works (reduced parameter displacement/trajectory length during optimization, shown via explicit motion analysis in Fig. 4 and video visualizations).

Reasonably strong reproducibility support: notation table, detailed hyperparameter and runtime breakdowns in the supplement, per-scene results, and additional sparse-view and front-facing/synthetic scene experiments extending generality of findings.
weaknesses: The core idea largely repackages existing pieces (dense 2D matching networks such as RoMa, multi-view triangulation, and Gaussian initialization) into a pipeline; the main novel elements are the sampling-distribution design and SH initialization via least squares, which are comparatively incremental compared to the strong empirical claims made in the abstract/intro ("fundamentally different approach").

Reliance on a pretrained dense matching model (RoMa) as an essential precondition for the method's success is a hidden but consequential dependency; the paper only briefly tests robustness to noise and other matchers (Tab. 5), but does not discuss failure cases where dense matching itself is unreliable (e.g., textureless regions, repetitive patterns, dynamic content, or very sparse view overlap) beyond a limited sparse-view supplement.

Reported speed/timing comparisons partly depend on reproducibility of baselines run on different or matched hardware conventions (footnotes indicate some numbers taken directly from other papers with different GPUs, e.g., A6000/RTX3090 vs A100), which slightly weakens the fairness of head-to-head training-time claims in Tab. 1-2.

The initialization step itself is not negligible in cost (dense matching over up to 180 reference views, ~120s described in supplement), and although this is included in reported times, the trade-off between correspondence computation and rendering time is not deeply analyzed for very large or many-image scenes, raising scalability questions not fully addressed.

Some ablation/robustness figures (e.g., Fig. 6 parameter sensitivity, Fig. 7 noise robustness) are aggregated/qualitative curves without confidence intervals or variance across scenes, making it hard to assess statistical significance of marginal gains.

The claim that EDGS "eliminates the need for densification entirely" is somewhat undercut by the paper's own experiments showing that combining EDGS initialization with ADC methods (Tab. 3) yields further improvements, suggesting densification still has residual benefit and the framing could be more calibrated.

Presentation issues: derivation in Sec 3.3 (Eqs. 4-7) is somewhat verbose for a standard DLT triangulation, taking space that could instead clarify how outlier correspondences and dynamic/textureless regions are handled; some numbers in tables (e.g., ScaffoldGS mean value changes) are explained only briefly, raising minor concerns about strict comparability with originally reported baselines.

strengths: The core idea—replacing incremental densification in 3DGS with a dense, correspondence-based initialization—is clean and well-motivated, and the paper provides a fairly complete pipeline (triangulation, confidence/geometry-based sampling, SH initialization).

Extensive ablation studies (Tab. 6, Figs. 4-7) probe individual components (sampling distribution terms, SH initialization, matching algorithm choice, robustness to initialization noise), which strengthens the mechanistic understanding of why the method works.

Compatibility experiments (Tab. 3, using EDGS as initialization for AbsGS, Mip-Splatting, 3DGS-MCMC, ScaffoldGS, RAIN-GS) show the initialization is a plausible plug-and-play component rather than a standalone competing pipeline, which is a practically useful framing.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough (sparse-view evaluation, per-scene tables, noise robustness, nearest-neighbor aggregation visualization, video results), improving reproducibility and transparency about limitations.
weaknesses: The method is not self-contained: it depends critically on a pretrained dense correspondence network (RoMa) and known camera poses. The ablation in Tab. 5 shows RAFT fails badly, indicating the approach's quality is tightly coupled to the choice/quality of an external matcher, which is not analyzed for generalization to more challenging scenes (repetitive textures, low overlap, dynamic content) beyond the benchmark datasets used.

Quantitative gains are mixed rather than uniformly superior. On Mip-NeRF360 (Tab. 1), EDGS+3DGS is not best on SSIM (0.839 vs 3DGS-MCMC's 0.842) or on some other cells, and improvements over strong recent baselines (3DGS-MCMC, ScaffoldGS) are often marginal (e.g., LPIPS 0.141 vs 0.176/0.179, but PSNR/SSIM close or slightly worse), undercutting the claim of matching or exceeding quality-focused SOTA across the board.

The reported 'training time' comparisons are somewhat favorable framings: the matching/triangulation preprocessing (≈120s per scene per the supplementary, dominated by 180×2 forward passes of a heavy network) is a substantial fixed cost that does not obviously amortize for smaller scenes or few-view settings, and the paper's headline speed claims (Fig. 1) could give a skewed impression if this preprocessing cost is not prominently reflected in the main figures.

The improvement narrative rests heavily on Tanks&Temples, Mip-NeRF360, and Deep Blending, a now-standard but limited benchmark suite; no evaluation on larger-scale, unbounded, or dynamic scenes is provided, so claims of general applicability ('broadly applicable enhancement') are not fully substantiated by the presented evidence.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: some ablation and per-scene tables in the supplementary (e.g., Tab. A2, Tab. 7) contain inconsistent or seemingly implausible values (e.g., very low ScaffoldGS PSNR in Tab. 1 relative to its SSIM/LPIPS, or the YGGT/YGGT-X comparison in Tab. 7 lacking sufficient methodological detail) that are not explained, making it harder to fully trust the reported numbers without independent verification.

The theoretical contribution is incremental relative to prior triangulation/initialization works (e.g., RadSplat, GaussianPro) — the novelty largely lies in the specific sampling/aggregation heuristics (confidence + reprojection thresholds) rather than a fundamentally new geometric or optimization principle, and the paper does not clearly delineate what specifically differentiates its geometric formulation from standard multi-view triangulation pipelines beyond engineering choices.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: replacing the slow, incremental densification of 3DGS with a one-shot dense initialization derived from triangulated dense 2D correspondences across multiple views, directly addressing a known inefficiency in the 3DGS pipeline.

Comprehensive experimental validation across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending), with results reported for both full convergence and early-stopping settings, showing competitive or superior quality with substantially reduced training time.

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies: sampling distribution components, SH initialization, matching algorithm choice (RoMa, LoFTR, DKM, RAFT), robustness to initialization noise, hyperparameter sensitivity, and comparison to naive initialization variants (denser COLMAP, random, depth-based, VGGT).

Demonstrated plug-and-play compatibility with existing adaptive density control methods (AbsGS, Mini-Splatting, 3DGS-MCMC, Scaffold-GS), showing the initialization is a complementary, broadly useful component rather than a standalone competitor.

Additional analyses that strengthen the mechanistic claims, e.g., Gaussian motion/displacement/trajectory-length analysis (Fig. 4) showing shorter optimization paths, and extreme-viewpoint rendering results showing reduced stretched-Gaussian artifacts.
Supplementary material is thorough, including sparse-view evaluation, per-scene breakdowns, notation table, and implementation details (timing breakdown, memory usage), aiding reproducibility.
Clear writing and figures that effectively communicate the core intuition (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) and support the claims with both qualitative and quantitative evidence.
weaknesses: The dense correspondence estimation and triangulation/SH-fitting steps rely on a pretrained matching network (RoMa) and add non-trivial preprocessing cost (~120s per scene per supplementary Sec. A); while this is reported, more discussion of scalability to very large scenes or many views (memory/time growth trends) would strengthen the efficiency claims.

Method depends on having enough view overlap/baseline for reliable dense correspondences and triangulation; performance on scenes with sparse or unevenly distributed cameras beyond the tested sparse-view setting (Sec. B) is not deeply analyzed, and failure modes of the correspondence step (e.g., textureless regions, repetitive structures) are not discussed in the main text.

Table 1 comparisons mix reported numbers from original papers with re-evaluated ones (footnotes indicate different GPUs for some baselines), which slightly complicates direct comparison of timing and could be clarified with unified hardware where feasible.

The improvement margins over strong recent baselines (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC, Scaffold-GS) in Table 1 are sometimes modest on some metrics, and the paper's main gains are more evident in early-training/speed regimes (Table 2) than in final asymptotic quality, which is worth being explicit about in the claims.

The hyperparameter selection (180 reference views, 2 neighbors, 20k correspondences) appears tuned empirically via saturation curves (Fig. 6) on the same benchmark used for evaluation; a held-out validation protocol for hyperparameter selection is not clearly described, raising minor concern about overfitting to the test datasets.
